title: ERP Systems: The Digital Backbone
description: Enterprise Resource Planning systems (SAP, Oracle, NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics) integrate the company’s core transactions — finance, procurement, inventory, manufacturing, HR — into one database with one process model. The promise: one version of the truth (the inventory number finance sees is the number operations sees), process discipline (the system enforces the approved workflow), and scale (transactions that drown spreadsheets flow through). The reality: ERP implementations are the most failure-prone projects in enterprise IT — the Standish data and the case-study graveyard (Hershey’s Halloween, Nike’s $100M write-down) show why: big-bang go-lives, underestimated change management, and customization that destroys upgradeability. The disciplines that succeed: process-first design (fix the process, then configure — never customize the software to broken processes), phased rollout (one module, one site at a time), executive ownership (the CEO’s project, not IT’s), and the 80/20 configuration rule (adopt the vanilla process unless the difference is strategic). Cloud ERP (NetSuite, Dynamics 365, S/4HANA Cloud) lowered the entry cost but not the change-management requirement.
key_points: One database, one process model across functions
Implementations are the most failure-prone IT projects
Process first, then configure; never customize to broken process
Phased rollout; executive ownership; 80/20 vanilla
how_it_works: Map processes, configure vanilla, phase the rollout, train deeply, govern master data, upgrade continuously.
best_fit: Companies outgrowing spreadsheet operations.

title: SOP Systems: Writing the Company Down
description: Standard Operating Procedures are the company written down — the system that lets the business run without the founder in the room. The SOP system has layers: policies (the rules — what must/must not happen), procedures (the steps — how it happens), work instructions (the detail — exactly how, with tolerances), and forms/checklists (the evidence — proof it happened). The writing discipline: procedures written by the people who do the work (accuracy), in the order performed (usability), with the why behind non-obvious steps (improvability), tested by a newcomer following them cold (the validation). The maintenance discipline: owners per SOP, review cycles (yearly or on change), version control, and the retirement of dead SOPs (the binder of obsolete procedures teaches contempt). The digital shift: video SOPs (phone-recorded demonstrations beat text for physical work), wiki-based living documents, and checklist apps. The test: can the business onboard a competent stranger to each role from the SOPs? If yes, the company is a system; if no, it is a collection of people.
key_points: Layers: policies, procedures, work instructions, checklists
Written by doers; tested by newcomers cold
Owners, review cycles, version control, retirements
Video SOPs beat text for physical work
how_it_works: Document with doers, validate with newcomers, assign owners, review cyclically, digitize where it helps.
best_fit: Any company that must outlive its founders’ memory.
t: SOP Systems: Writing the Company Down

title: Knowledge Management Systems
description: Knowledge management prevents the company from re-learning everything with each departure: the system for capturing, organizing, and reusing what the organization knows. The architecture: the wiki/intranet (the searchable record — decisions, how-tos, project histories), the experts directory (who knows what — the fastest knowledge system ever built), communities of practice (the living networks where tacit knowledge moves), and the lessons-learned discipline (project retrospectives captured, indexed, and actually consulted). The capture disciplines: write decisions with context (the decision log — what, why, alternatives rejected), document the non-obvious (the troubleshooting guide for the error that took three days), and record the customer knowledge (the CRM as institutional memory). The cultural prerequisites: time to write (the 10% rule — knowledge work needs documentation time), recognition for contributors, and leaders who consult the wiki visibly. The failure: the wiki nobody reads because nobody writes because nobody reads — broken by seeding content and linking it into workflows.
key_points: Wiki, experts directory, communities, lessons-learned
Decision logs with context and rejected alternatives
Cultural prerequisites: time, recognition, visible use
Seed content and link into workflows to break the cycle
how_it_works: Build the wiki, map the experts, run communities, capture lessons, recognize contributors, integrate into work.
best_fit: Knowledge-work companies of any scale.

title: Onboarding Systems
description: Onboarding determines whether new hires become productive in weeks or quarters — and whether they stay. The system: pre-boarding (equipment, accounts, and the welcome before day one — the hire who waits three days for a laptop learns the company’s priorities), the first-week plan (the buddy, the stakeholder meetings, the first small win — momentum matters), the 30-60-90 plan (learning goals per phase, co-written with the manager), role training (the SOPs, the tools, the customers), culture transmission (the values in action — stories, not slides), and the feedback loops (week-one, month-one, and 90-day check-ins asking what confused them — the confusion inventory improves the system). The metrics: time to productivity (by role), 90-day retention, and new-hire satisfaction. The research: structured onboarding improves retention dramatically (the oft-cited 82% figure reflects real effects). The failure: the “HR orientation plus good luck” — paperwork without integration. Onboarding is the company’s first impression as an employer; design it like one.
key_points: Pre-boarding: equipment and accounts before day one
30-60-90 plans co-written with managers
Culture via stories, not slides
Metrics: time to productivity, 90-day retention
how_it_works: Prepare before day one, buddy up, plan 30-60-90, train the role, transmit culture, check in and improve.
best_fit: Any company hiring regularly.

title: Performance Management Systems
description: Performance management — the system for aligning, assessing, and developing people — has been reinvented after decades of annual-review failure. The modern system: continuous feedback (regular 1:1s with coaching, not yearly judgment), clear goals (OKRs or equivalent — the alignment layer), periodic reviews (quarterly or twice-yearly — lighter, forward-looking), calibration (managers aligning ratings across teams — the fairness mechanism), and development planning (the growth conversation separate from the rating conversation). The rating debate: many companies dropped numerical ratings (the demotivation and gaming they caused) while keeping differentiation (performance must still affect pay and promotion — the honesty requirement). The disciplines: train managers in feedback and coaching (the system is only as good as its managers), separate development from evaluation conversations, and act on the results (low performers managed out kindly but firmly — the team watches what happens). The test: do employees know where they stand and how to grow? If yes, the system works regardless of its form.
key_points: Continuous feedback plus periodic forward-looking reviews
Calibration aligns fairness across teams
Separate development from evaluation conversations
Act on results — the team watches
how_it_works: Set goals, run 1:1s, review periodically, calibrate, plan development, differentiate rewards, manage out kindly.
best_fit: Any company with employees to develop.

title: Hiring Systems
description: Hiring is the highest-leverage system in the company — every hire shapes the culture and capability for years. The structured system: the scorecard (the role’s mission, outcomes, and competencies defined before sourcing — hiring without a scorecard is shopping without a list), structured interviews (same questions per candidate, scored rubrics — the validity research is clear: structured beats unstructured dramatically), work samples (the closest predictor — do the actual work), reference checks (done properly: backchannel plus provided, asking about specific behaviors), and the hiring committee (the decision by group, not the manager alone — de-biasing). The disciplines: speed (top candidates decide in weeks — the slow process loses them), the bar-raiser (someone outside the team guarding the standard), and the close (selling the candidate — hiring is mutual). The metrics: quality of hire (hiring-manager satisfaction at 6–12 months), time to fill, offer acceptance, and early attrition. The rule: hire slowly for values and capability, and never lower the bar for urgency — the urgent hire is the expensive mistake.
key_points: Scorecard before sourcing; structured interviews with rubrics
Work samples predict best; committees de-bias
Speed matters — top candidates decide in weeks
Never lower the bar for urgency
how_it_works: Scorecard, source, screen, structured interview, work sample, references, committee decision, close fast.
best_fit: Every company — the universal leverage point.

title: The Operating Cadence: Annual to Daily
description: The operating cadence — the company’s full rhythm from annual to daily — is the process system that synchronizes everything. The annual: strategy review and budget (the year’s direction and resources, 2–3 days). The quarterly: business review and planning (score the quarter, set the next — the 90-day heartbeat). The monthly: operational review (metrics deep-dive, one strategic topic). The weekly: execution cadence (Level 10 style — scorecard, priorities, issues). The daily: huddles where needed (15 minutes, blockers). The design disciplines: each layer has a fixed agenda and owner, layers connect (the weekly executes the quarterly plan; the quarterly serves the annual strategy), the calendar is published yearly (rhythms beat ad-hoc), and every layer earns its time (the ROI review). The failure: cadence as calendar-filling — meetings multiplying without purpose. The test: trace any weekly discussion up to the annual strategy — the connected cadence tells the story; the disconnected one cannot. Rhythm is the cheapest coordination technology ever invented.
key_points: Annual strategy to daily huddles: the full stack
Fixed agendas and owners per layer
Layers connect: weekly serves quarterly serves annual
Published yearly calendar; every layer earns its time
how_it_works: Design the layer stack, publish the calendar, run fixed agendas, connect plans across layers, review ROI.
best_fit: Any operating company.
t: The Operating Cadence: Annual to Daily

title: Budgeting and Forecasting Systems
description: Budgeting translates strategy into resource allocation — and most budgeting systems do it badly. The traditional annual budget: negotiated the prior fall, obsolete by March, gaming-intensive (spend it or lose it, sandbagged targets). The better systems: rolling forecasts (the next 4–6 quarters reforecast quarterly — always looking forward, never defending the obsolete), driver-based planning (the few variables that actually move the business — headcount, conversion, price), beyond-budgeting principles (devolved decisions, relative targets, fast resource reallocation — the Handelsbanken/Svenska model), and zero-based reviews for big cost categories (justify, don’t inherit). The disciplines: separate targets (aspirational), forecasts (expected), and resource allocation (committed) — conflating them corrupts all three; review monthly with variance analysis that asks why, not who; and keep the process fast (the 3-month budget ordeal costs more than it allocates). The test: can resources move to the opportunity mid-year? If not, the budget is a cage.
key_points: Annual budgets obsolete fast; rolling forecasts stay live
Separate targets, forecasts, and allocations
Driver-based: the few variables that move the business
Resources must move to opportunity mid-year
how_it_works: Forecast rolling, plan by drivers, review monthly, reallocate fast, zero-base the big categories periodically.
best_fit: Companies needing real resource agility.

title: CRM and Revenue Operations
description: Customer Relationship Management systems (Salesforce, HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics) are the revenue organization’s system of record — and revenue operations (RevOps) is the discipline of running them as one system across marketing, sales, and success. The architecture: the unified data model (one account, one contact, one opportunity definition — the definitions are the system), the funnel instrumentation (stage definitions, conversion metrics, velocity — the physics of the pipeline), the process automation (lead routing, approval flows, renewal triggers), and the forecasting discipline (commit/best-case/pipeline with inspection cadence). The RevOps disciplines: one ops team for the full funnel (ending the marketing-vs-sales data wars), the tech stack rationalized (the 15-tool stack nobody integrated), and the metrics that matter (CAC, LTV, payback, NRR — the unit economics). The failure: CRM as expensive address book — data entered for management, never used for decisions. The test: does the forecast come from the system or from reps’ optimism? The system’s forecast is the honest one.
key_points: One data model across marketing, sales, success
Funnel instrumentation: stages, conversion, velocity
RevOps unifies the full-funnel operations
Forecast from the system, not optimism
how_it_works: Unify the data model, instrument stages, automate routing, inspect forecasts, align on unit economics.
best_fit: B2B revenue organizations.

title: The Tech Stack as Process System
description: The company’s software stack is its process system made executable — and stack sprawl is process chaos made expensive. The architecture disciplines: the system of record per domain (one CRM, one ERP, one HRIS — duplicates are the sprawl), integration over islands (APIs and iPaaS connecting the records — the employee re-typing data between systems is the failure signal), the collaboration layer (the chat/docs/video where work actually happens — standardized, not 6 overlapping tools), and the security layer (SSO, device management, data classification — the stack’s immune system). The governance: the tech council (who approves new tools — the shadow-IT prevention), the stack review (yearly: what do we actually use?), and the total-cost view (licenses plus integration plus admin — the $10/user tool with $50/user admin cost). The principle: every tool should eliminate work greater than its own administration. The test: count the logins — the employee with 30 logins works for the stack, not with it.
key_points: One system of record per domain
Integration over islands; re-typing is the failure signal
Standardized collaboration layer
Every tool must eliminate more work than its admin
core_principles: Work with the stack, not for it
how_it_works: Declare records, integrate via APIs, standardize collaboration, govern additions, review yearly.
best_fit: Any company with more than a dozen tools.
t: The Tech Stack as Process System

title: Document and Record Management
description: Document management — the unglamorous system that decides whether the company can find its own knowledge — runs on boring disciplines done consistently. The architecture: the taxonomy (the folder/ tagging structure — designed once, governed always; the organic taxonomy becomes the junk drawer), naming conventions (the date-first, project-first patterns that make search work), version control (one current version, history preserved — the “final_v7_REAL” filename is the failure), access control (who sees what — the ex-employee with the drive access is the breach), and retention (what gets kept, what gets destroyed, on what schedule — the legal requirement and the sanity measure). The disciplines: the librarian function (someone owns the taxonomy — part-time is fine, nobody is not), the migration discipline (new systems inherit organized content, not dumps), and the search test (can a newcomer find the thing?). The payoff: institutional memory that survives turnover. The cost of neglect: the company that cannot find its own contracts.
key_points: Taxonomy designed once, governed always
Naming conventions make search work
One current version; access controlled; retention scheduled
The librarian function: someone owns it
how_it_works: Design taxonomy, set conventions, control versions and access, schedule retention, assign ownership.
best_fit: Any company producing documents.

title: Internal Communications Systems
description: Internal communication is the company’s nervous system — and most companies’ is inflamed. The architecture: the channels with purposes (chat for quick coordination, email for formal/external, wiki for durable knowledge, all-hands for alignment — the channel confusion is the disease), the writing culture (memos over meetings for decisions — the Amazon six-pager discipline; async updates over status meetings), the leadership communication rhythm (the weekly/monthly note — what’s happening, why it matters, what’s next), and the feedback channels (upward — the AMA, the survey, the skip-level — because the nervous system must sense upward too). The disciplines: default to written (writing clarifies thinking and scales reading), default to public channels (the DM culture hides information), and measure the load (the employee drowning in notifications is not informed — they are interrupted). The test: can a returning-from-vacation employee catch up in an hour from the written record? If yes, the system works.
key_points: Channels with purposes; end channel confusion
Memos over meetings for decisions
Leadership rhythm: what, why, next
Upward sensing: AMAs, surveys, skip-levels
how_it_works: Define channel purposes, build writing culture, run leadership rhythm, open upward channels, measure load.
best_fit: Any company above ~20 people.

title: Procurement and Vendor Management
description: Procurement — how the company buys — is a process system with direct P&L impact: well-run procurement saves 5–15% of addressable spend. The system: the requisition-to-pay flow (request, approval by threshold, PO, receipt, invoice match, payment — the controls that prevent fraud and waste), strategic sourcing (category strategies, competitive bidding, total-cost analysis — not just price), vendor management (scorecards, business reviews, the preferred-vendor list), and the controls (segregation of duties — the requester cannot approve; approval thresholds; the audit trail). The disciplines: spend visibility (you cannot manage what you cannot see — the spend cube by category and vendor), the 80/20 vendor focus (deep relationships with the critical few, market pricing for the rest), and the maverick-spend war (the off-contract buying that destroys leverage — controlled by making the approved path the easy path). The ethics: gift policies, conflict disclosure, rotation on big categories — procurement without integrity is a scandal waiting. The test: what did we save versus market last year, documented?
key_points: Requisition-to-pay flow with threshold approvals
Strategic sourcing: total cost, not just price
Spend visibility; 80/20 vendor focus
Make the approved path the easy path
how_it_works: Map spend, build category strategies, run competitive sourcing, manage vendors, control the flow, audit.
best_fit: Any company with material external spend.

title: Quality Management Systems (ISO 9001)
description: ISO 9001 — the world’s most adopted management standard (1M+ certified organizations) — is a process system for consistent quality: the quality manual, documented procedures, and the plan-do-check-act cycle audited by third parties. The requirements: context and leadership (quality as management’s job), risk-based thinking (what could go wrong — addressed proportionally), documented processes with owners, measurement and monitoring, internal audits, management review, and corrective action on nonconformities. The value when done right: the discipline of writing processes down, measuring them, and improving them — customers’ trust (certification as a market signal), and the audit as a free consulting engagement. The failure when done wrong: the certificate on the wall with the binder nobody opens — documentation theater for the auditor. The disciplines that separate the two: processes written by doers, audits that find real issues, management reviews that change things. The test: would you run the system without the certificate? If yes, it is real.
key_points: Plan-do-check-act; documented processes; third-party audited
Risk-based thinking; corrective action discipline
Value: trust signal plus real process discipline
Theater version: binder nobody opens
core_principles: Run it for the business, not the certificate
how_it_works: Document processes, implement with owners, audit internally, review with management, correct, certify, improve.
best_fit: Companies where quality consistency is commercial.

title: Safety Management Systems
description: Safety management systems (ISO 45001, OSHA VPP, the energy industry’s OMS) organize the company’s duty of care into a process system: hazard identification and risk assessment (the job safety analyses, the HAZOPs — the work of seeing dangers before they bite), controls hierarchy (elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE — in that order, always), incident reporting and investigation (every incident and near-miss — the near-miss reporting rate is the culture metric), training and competence (verified, not just delivered), and the management review (leadership owning safety performance). The cultural disciplines: stop-work authority (anyone stops unsafe work — protected, celebrated), the just culture (honest mistakes vs reckless violations — distinguished fairly), and leading indicators (near-miss rates, audit findings, training completion — managed before the lagging injury rates). The economics: the best safety performers are also the best operational performers — discipline transfers. The test: what happens to the messenger? In a working safety system, the reporter is thanked.
key_points: Hazard ID; controls hierarchy; incident investigation
Stop-work authority for everyone, protected
Just culture: honest mistakes vs violations
Leading indicators managed before lagging
how_it_works: Assess hazards, apply controls hierarchy, train and verify, investigate everything, review with leadership.
best_fit: Any company with physical operational risk.

title: Innovation Process Systems
description: Innovation needs process too — the managed pipeline from idea to scale. The stage-gate pipeline (Cooper): idea capture, scoping, business case, development, testing, launch — with kill decisions at gates (the portfolio’s discipline). The venture model: internal startups with funding stages, metrics, and the same pivot-or-persevere rigor as external ventures. The ambidextrous setup: the explore unit separated from core processes (different metrics, different governance — the core’s stage-gates would kill ventures). The idea systems: the capture mechanism (everyone can submit — the system that evaluates fast), the hackathon/innovation time (the slack where ideas form — 3M’s 15%, Google’s 20% mythology and reality), and the internal venture fund. The disciplines: portfolio thinking (most ideas fail — the portfolio must contain the failures), fast cheap experiments (the lean startup inside), and the scaling path (the venture that works needs the core’s muscle — designed handoff). The failure: the innovation theater — labs, posters, and zero launches.
key_points: Pipeline: capture to launch with kill gates
Venture model: staged funding, pivot-or-persevere
Explore separated from core processes
Portfolio thinking contains the failures
core_principles: Manage the portfolio, not just projects
how_it_works: Capture ideas, stage-gate or venture-fund them, experiment fast, kill fast, scale winners via designed handoff.
best_fit: Companies needing systematic innovation.

title: Customer Feedback and Voice-of-Customer Systems
description: Voice-of-customer systems turn customer reality into operational input — the companies that systematize listening outperform those that listen sporadically. The instruments: NPS/CSAT/CES measurement (the relationship, satisfaction, and effort scores — trended, not worshipped), the closed-loop process (every detractor gets a follow-up — the loop that turns measurement into recovery), win/loss analysis (why deals close or die — the product’s honest mirror), customer advisory boards (the deep qualitative channel), and the frontline intelligence system (support tickets, sales notes, reviews — mined systematically, not anecdotally). The disciplines: the feedback goes somewhere (the product backlog, the process review — the black hole teaches customers silence), the loop closes visibly (customers told what changed because they spoke), and the metrics connect to action (the NPS owner with the improvement budget). The failure: the survey industrial complex — measured exhaustively, acted on never. The test: name three things that changed last quarter because customers said so.
key_points: NPS/CSAT/CES trended; closed-loop detractor follow-up
Win/loss as the product’s honest mirror
Feedback must reach the backlog — no black holes
Name three changes customers caused last quarter
how_it_works: Measure, route feedback to owners, act, close loops with customers, track what changed.
best_fit: Any company with customers to keep.

title: The Planning Cascade: From Strategy to Task
description: The planning cascade connects the decade to the day — the process system that keeps daily work serving strategy. The layers: the BHAG/vision (the decade’s direction), the 3-year picture (the vivid strategic destination), the 1-year plan (the annual objectives and budget), the quarterly priorities (the rocks — 3–7, owned), the weekly execution (the cadence that moves the rocks), the daily focus (the huddle, the calendar — the individual’s hours). The disciplines: each layer derives from the one above (the quarterly rock that serves no annual objective is the wrong rock), each layer is written and visible (the cascade in people’s heads is folklore), and the review flows upward (the weekly issues inform the quarterly plan; the quarterly results test the strategy). The failure: the disconnected layers — strategy decks nobody executes, daily work nobody connects. The tool: the one-page plan per layer, linked explicitly. The test: ask anyone what they are doing this week and why — the cascade answers both.
key_points: BHAG to daily focus: the connected layers
Each layer derives from above; reviews flow upward
Written and visible at every layer
One-page plans, explicitly linked
how_it_works: Write each layer’s plan, link explicitly, execute downward, review upward, adjust.
best_fit: Companies wanting strategy in daily work.
t: The Planning Cascade: From Strategy to Task

title: Meeting Systems and Decision Logs
description: Meetings are expensive coordination — the system makes them worth it. The meeting architecture: the cadence (the recurring rhythms with fixed agendas), the decision meetings (called for specific decisions, with pre-reads — the memo before the meeting), the working sessions (collaboration, not status), and the 1:1s (the relationship infrastructure). The disciplines: the invite states purpose and pre-read (no purpose, no meeting), the smallest sufficient invite list (every attendee costs), the decision log (every decision: what, why, who, date — the organizational memory), the action log (owner and deadline per action — reviewed next time), and the no-meeting blocks (maker time protected). The decision log deserves emphasis: companies re-litigate decisions because nobody wrote them down — the log ends the “I thought we decided” tax. The review: the quarterly meeting audit (which meetings earn their hours?). The principle: meetings are for decisions and connection; everything else goes async.
key_points: Purpose and pre-read on every invite
Decision log: what, why, who, date
Action log with owners; reviewed next time
Quarterly meeting audit
how_it_works: Architect the cadence, enforce invite discipline, log decisions and actions, protect maker time, audit quarterly.
best_fit: Any company with meetings.

title: Process Mining and Operational Intelligence
description: Process mining — analyzing event logs to discover how work actually flows — brings X-ray vision to process systems: the discovered process (mined from ERP/CRM/ticket logs) versus the designed process (the SOP), with the conformance gap showing where reality diverges. The applications: bottleneck discovery (where cases actually wait), variant analysis (the 20 ways the “standard” process really runs), compliance checking (did the required approvals happen?), and automation targeting (the high-volume variants worth automating). The disciplines: data quality first (the logs must capture the events — instrumentation before insight), the process owner’s involvement (the miner finds the what; the owner knows the why), and the improvement loop (mine, improve, re-mine — the continuous version). The tools (Celonis and followers) matured from research to enterprise standard. The caution: surveillance perception — mining individual performance without trust destroys the culture the improvement needs. Mine the process, not the person.
key_points: Discovered vs designed process; the conformance gap
Bottlenecks, variants, compliance, automation targets
Data quality before insight
Mine the process, not the person
how_it_works: Instrument event logs, mine the actual flow, analyze with owners, improve, re-mine continuously.
best_fit: Transaction-heavy operations with event logs.

title: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery
description: Business continuity — the process system for surviving disruption — separates companies that bend from companies that break. The system: business impact analysis (which processes matter, how long each can be down — the RTO/RPO per process), the continuity plans (the playbooks per scenario: facility loss, IT outage, supply disruption, pandemic — specific, assigned, tested), disaster recovery for IT (backups tested by restore, not by backup log — the restore that never ran is the backup that fails), crisis communication (who tells whom, in what order — employees first, always), and the exercise program (tabletops yearly, full simulations for the critical scenarios). The disciplines: the plan owner per scenario (the binder nobody owns is fiction), the tested restore (quarterly for critical systems), and the post-incident review (every disruption improves the plan). The economics: continuity costs 1–2% of revenue to do well; one existential disruption costs the company. The test: when did you last exercise? The untested plan is a hope.
key_points: Impact analysis: RTO/RPO per process
Playbooks per scenario: assigned, specific, tested
Backups proven by restore, not by log
Exercise yearly; review every disruption
how_it_works: Analyze impacts, write playbooks, assign owners, test restores, exercise yearly, improve per incident.
best_fit: Any company that must survive disruption.

title: The Process Audit: Keeping Systems Honest
description: Process systems decay without audits — the process audit is the maintenance. The audit types: the compliance audit (are we following the process? — the ISO-style check), the effectiveness audit (does the process achieve its purpose? — the harder question), and the efficiency audit (could the process cost less? — the lean question). The method: sample the work (not everything — the representative sample), trace it through the process (the walk-through), interview the doers (the workarounds reveal the truth), and score against the standard. The disciplines: audit for improvement, not punishment (the punitive audit teaches concealment), publish findings with owners and deadlines (the audit without actions is observation), and track the actions to closure (the follow-up is the audit’s product). The cadence: critical processes yearly, others on rotation, plus triggered audits (after incidents, before certifications). The principle: the process audit is how the system talks to itself — honestly, regularly, and with consequences for the findings.
key_points: Compliance, effectiveness, efficiency: the three audits
Sample, trace, interview doers
Audit for improvement, never punishment
Actions tracked to closure
how_it_works: Schedule audits, sample and trace, interview, publish findings with owners, track closure.
best_fit: Any company with process systems worth keeping.
t: The Process Audit: Keeping Systems Honest

title: Scaling Process Systems with Growth
description: Process systems must evolve with headcount — the system that served 20 strangles 200. The scaling stages: tribal (under ~15 — the founder’s head holds the processes), documented (15–50 — write the critical 20 processes before the knowledge walks out), systematized (50–200 — owners, metrics, and tools per process; the ERP/CRM era), governed (200+ — process architecture, audits, continuous improvement as functions). The transition disciplines: document before the pain (the process written calmly beats the one written in crisis), hire the process owners (the first ops hire is the highest-leverage hire of the stage), and resist over-systematizing early (the 20-person company with ISO 9001 has mistaken motion for progress). The warning signs of lag: the workarounds everyone knows, the onboarding that takes months, the “ask Sarah” dependencies. The rule: systematize one stage ahead of pain, never two — the process system should feel slightly light, not slightly heavy.
key_points: Tribal, documented, systematized, governed: the stages
Document the critical 20 before knowledge walks out
Hire process owners at each transition
One stage ahead of pain, never two
how_it_works: Assess the stage, document the critical processes, hire owners, install tools, govern lightly, review per stage.
best_fit: Growing companies at each transition.

title: The Process Owner Role
description: Every important process needs an owner — the person accountable for the process working, not just for doing their step. The role’s accountabilities: the process performs (metrics owned and reviewed), the process is documented and current (the SOP lives), the process improves (the kaizen never stops), and the process’s people are capable (trained, coached). The authority the role needs: to change the process (within guardrails), to convene its participants, to escalate blockers — authority without these is title without teeth. The common failure: the process owner as an extra duty on an overloaded manager — the process gets the leftover attention, which is none. The design: significant processes get dedicated or primary-duty owners; the owner’s performance review includes process metrics; owners meet as a community (the process council — sharing improvements across processes). The principle: processes without owners decay; owners without authority frustrate; the pair sustains. Name an owner for every process that matters — the unnamed process is the unmanaged one.
key_points: Accountable for the process working, not just their step
Needs change authority, convening power, escalation rights
Extra-duty ownership fails — the process gets leftovers
Owners’ reviews include process metrics
how_it_works: Name owners for key processes, grant real authority, review on process metrics, convene the owner community.
best_fit: Any company with processes that matter.
